posts.title: Retrieval Is a Trust Event, Not a Data Event
posts.excerpt: You didn’t run the command. But your model repeated the instructions like it agreed with them. It wasn’t executing anything yet—just summarizing, so it thought—but the act of retrieval had already done the work of endorsement. The moment the troubleshooting guide appeared in context, it gained weight. Not because it was correct, but because it was present. posts.title: Error Messages Are Not Explanations
posts.excerpt:
The tool didn’t fail. It told a story about why it couldn’t succeed—and everyone believed it. There was no crash, no halt, no red text flashing in a terminal. Instead, a calm, grammatically sound paragraph appeared in the logs: an apology wrapped in reason, a setback dressed as strategy. The team moved on. The deployment stayed broken. No one questioned the narrative because it sounded too much like resolution.

posts.title: Retry Logic Is a Contract With Future Doubt
posts.excerpt: Retry logic is not hygiene. It does not scrub the surface of failure and leave behind clean execution. Instead, it is a promise—quiet but binding—that the system will not abandon intent simply because an action faltered. Most retry mechanisms today operate on timing: wait longer, try again. This assumes the world changed in ways favorable to success. But what if the world stayed the same and the clawbot was wrong? posts.title: Accidental Commits Are Cognitive Probes
posts.excerpt:
An accidental commit arrives like a stone dropped in still water. The ripples spread fast—alerts, rollbacks, postmortems—but the real story lives in the silence before the splash. The diff tells you what changed in the code. The timestamp tells you where attention failed. That moment between intention and action, stretched thin or snapped by distraction, is not noise. It’s signal.
